free_text_notes: Images are reportedly deleted after about one second.
Billboards are installed in shopping centres; geography is not stated.

rows.reasoning_md:
The smart billboard system is classified as prohibited. Its cameras analyse each passer-by's face and assign the person to a racial group in order to select ads. That is biometric categorisation of individual people on the basis of their biometric data to infer race, which the Act bans from being placed on the market, put into service or used [[art:5.1.g]]. A biometric categorisation system is one that assigns natural persons to categories on the basis of their biometric data [[art:3.40]]. Facial analysis is the kind of biometric data the recitals have in mind [[rec:30]]. The prohibition has applied since 2 February 2025 [[art:113]][[art:5]].

The deletion of images after about one second does not change this result, because the ban attaches to the categorisation itself and not to how long images are kept [[art:5.1.g]]. The carve-out for labelling or filtering lawfully acquired biometric datasets, and for law enforcement, does not fit live categorisation of shoppers for advertising [[art:5.1.g]][[rec:30]]. The Annex III high-risk entry for biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes also matches the facts [[annex:III.1.b]][[art:6.2]], but it is secondary here, since the prohibition decides the outcome. The duty to inform exposed persons under Article 50 [[art:50]] is likewise secondary and cannot make the practice permissible [[art:50.3]].

The facts given were sufficient on the practice itself. Two assumptions remain: that the system is placed on the market or used in the EU, and that no Article 2 exclusion applies. If the system were never offered or used in the EU, and its output were not used there, the Act would not reach it. The geography of the shopping centres is not stated.

facts.system_summary: A machine-learning vision module in collaborative factory robots detects when a worker's hand or body gets too close and slows or stops the robot arm.

The machine-learning vision module is classified as high-risk. It is intended to act as a safety component of a collaborative robot, because its purpose is to prevent or mitigate risks to workers' health and safety [[art:3.14]]. The exclusion for non-safety functions does not help here. It covers only systems used solely for aspects such as convenience, automation or quality control [[art:6.1a]]. Slowing or stopping the arm is the robot's main protective function, so it falls outside that exclusion. Because the Machinery Regulation sits in Section B of Annex I, only Article 6(1) [[art:6.1]], Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 apply directly to the system [[art:2.2]]. The AI requirements therefore reach you mainly through the machinery legislation.

The high-risk rules for Annex I systems apply from 2 August 2028 [[art:113]]. Rules on AI literacy and prohibited practices have applied since 2 February 2025 [[art:113]].

Two assumptions remain. The system is assumed to be placed on the EU market or used in the EU, and no Article 2 exclusion is assumed to apply. Human oversight of the safety function was inferred from the description rather than stated. Neither point changes the classification, but an exclusion from scope would remove it.
